Ahiman
uh-HYE-man
proper noun
Hebrew Achiman (H289), commonly read brother of a gift or my brother is a gift — from ach (H251), brother, with a second element read as man, a portion or gift.

Biblical Definition

Ahiman was one of the three sons of Anak at Hebron, the giants whose presence broke the nerve of the ten spies. And they ascended by the south, and came unto Hebron; where Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, the children of Anak, were (Num 13:22). The report that followed described a land that ate up its inhabitants, and men beside whom the spies were as grasshoppers in their own sight. Caleb alone said Let us go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it (Num 13:30) — and forty-five years later, an old man of eighty-five, he asked for that mountain and got it: Caleb drove thence the three sons of Anak, Sheshai, and Ahiman, and Talmai (Jos 15:14). Judges records the same conquest from the tribe's side (Jdg 1:10). A second Ahiman is a porter of the house of God in the register of those who dwelt at Jerusalem (1Ch 9:17). The giant of Hebron is the standing biblical example of an obstacle that is real, that is correctly measured, and that is nevertheless beaten at the appointed time by a man who believed God about it.

Origin & Era

One of the three sons of Anak at Hebron, the giants who terrified the spies and were afterwards driven out by Caleb; also a porter after the captivity.

AHIMAN, Hebrew Achiman, commonly read brother of a gift.

1. One of the three sons of Anak dwelling at Hebron when the spies came.

Named with Sheshai and Talmai, the children of Anak.

Caleb drove the three sons of Anak from Hebron forty-five years later.

2. A porter of the house of God among those who dwelt at Jerusalem after the captivity.

Key Scripture

Num 13:22 — "And they ascended by the south, and came unto Hebron; where Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, the children of Anak, were. (Now Hebron was built seven years before Zoan in Egypt.)"

Jos 15:14 — "And Caleb drove thence the three sons of Anak, Sheshai, and Ahiman, and Talmai, the children of Anak."

Jdg 1:10 — "And Judah went against the Canaanites that dwelt in Hebron: (now the name of Hebron before was Kirjatharba:) and they slew Sheshai, and Ahiman, and Talmai."

1Ch 9:17 — "And the porters were, Shallum, and Akkub, and Talmon, and Ahiman, and their brethren: Shallum was the chief;"

Modern Corruption

Faith is presented as refusing to see the difficulty; Caleb saw the giants exactly as the other spies did, and drew the opposite conclusion.

expand to see more

A shallow account of faith makes it a kind of selective blindness — a determination not to look at the obstacle, to speak only positively, to deny the size of the giants. Numbers 13 will not support it. Caleb and Joshua walked the same forty days as the other ten, saw the same walled cities and the same sons of Anak at Hebron, and never once disputed the report of what was there. The difference was not in the survey. It was in a single omitted factor: the LORD is with us: fear them not (Num 14:9).

That is the shape of biblical faith everywhere. It counts the cost (Luk 14:28), it does not pretend the furnace is cool or the lions toothless, and it adds God to the arithmetic as the largest term. Caleb was eighty-five when he came back for Hebron and asked for the hardest ground in the inheritance, saying if so be the LORD will be with me, then I shall be able to drive them out (Jos 14:12). The principle to recover is that faith is realism with God included, and that the believer who has told himself the difficulty is smaller than it is has not exercised faith but avoided it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Achiman (H289), from ach (H251), brother, with a second element signifying a portion or gift.

expand to see more

Hebrew Achiman (H289) — a son of Anak (Num 13:22) and a porter after the captivity (1Ch 9:17).

Hebrew Anaq (H6061) — Anak, whose sons were the giants of Hebron; the children of Anak, which come of the giants (Num 13:33).

Hebrew nephilim (H5303) — giants, fallen ones; the word in the spies' report.

Hebrew Chebron (H2275) — Hebron, formerly Kirjath-arba, the city Caleb asked for and took.

Hebrew malé acharey — to follow fully; he hath wholly followed the LORD (Num 32:12), said of Caleb.

Usage

"“Where Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, the children of Anak, were”."

"“Caleb drove thence the three sons of Anak”."

"“Let us go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it” (Num 13:30)."
